text:
French philosophy - Wikipedia
Contents
French philosophy
French philosophy
is
philosophy
in the
French language
and by
French people
. French philosophy includes several schools of thought and has influenced
Western philosophy
as a whole for centuries. It includes the medieval
scholasticism
of
Peter Abelard
, the founding of
modern philosophy
by
René Descartes
, the 18th century
Enlightenment
philosophes
who influenced the
French Revolution
, 19th century eclecticism, spiritualism,
socialism
, and
positivism
; and 20th century
continental philosophy
such as
philosophy of science
,
phenomenology
,
existentialism
,
structuralism
,
poststructuralism
, and
postmodernism
.
Medieval period
French philosophy begins in the medieval period with
Latin
authors. The
Romanization
of
Gaul
brought Latin and
Gallo-Roman culture
.
Cassiodorus
(ca. 490–585) cites in his book
Variae
(dated 526) a letter to king
Athalaric
: "Finally you found Roman eloquence in regions that were not originally its own; and there the reading of
Cicero
rendered you eloquent where once the
Gaulish
language resounded."
[
1
]
Christian monk
Gennadius of Massilia
(died c. 496) was the author of
De Ecclesiasticis Dogmatibus
(
Of Church Doctrine
), long attributed to
Saint Augustine
.
[
2
]
[
3
]
Medieval philosophy
was very much a part of
Christian philosophy
and
theology
.
Ratramnus
(d. c. 868) defended
Gottschalk of Orbais
' (808–868) views on
double predestination
, a controversy throughout
Francia
in the 9th century.
[
4
]
Ratramnus also later supported Gottschalk in his conflict with archbishop
Hincmar
(806–882) of
Rheims
, advisor to
Charles the Bald
. Hincmar of Rheims altered a hymn, changing the words
trina deitas
(triune God) for
summa deitas
(supreme God).
[
5
]
[
6
]
Gottschalk accused Hincmar of
Sabellianism
, and Hincmar accused Gottschalk of
Arianism
.
[
7
]
Ratramnus also wrote
Against the Objections of the Greeks who Slandered the Roman Church
, a response to the
Photian schism
(863–867) and defense of the
filioque
addition to the
Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed
.
[
8
]
The
Benedictine
monk
of
Marmoutier Abbey
and
empiricist
Gaunilo
is well known for his work
In Behalf of the Fool
.
[
a
]
Gaunilo objects to Saint
Anselm of Canterbury
's (1033–1109)
ontological argument
for the
existence of God
found in Anselm's
Proslogion
(c. 1078). Gaunilo contends as a
reductio
that the same argument proves the existence of "the most perfect island".
[
9
]
Lanfranc
(c. 1010–1089) and Saint Anselm were Benedictine monks at
Bec Abbey
.
[
10
]
Medieval philosophy was also concerned with the
problem of universals
inherited from
antiquity
.
Roscellinus
(c. 1050–c. 1121) defended
nominalism
, stating universals are merely an emission of sound (
flatus vocis
).
[
11
]
[
12
]
Among Roscellinus' supporters was
Raimbert of Lille
.
[
13
]
Roscellinus also stated the three persons of
the Trinity
were not one substance, arguing if they were then
God the Father
and the
Holy Spirit
would have become incarnate along with
God the Son
. This prompted Anselm's
De Fide Trinitatis
.
[
b
]
In 1092/1093, a
council convoked at Soissons
by the
archbishop of Reims
condemned his interpretation and accused Roscellinus of
tritheism
.
[
16
]
[
17
]
Roscellinus recanted his theological beliefs, but later returned to professing them.
[
18
]
Anselm of Laon
(d. 1117) studied under Anselm at Bec and was a leading proponent of
philosophical realism
who helped to pioneer
biblical hermeneutics
.
[
19
]
William of Champeaux
(c. 1070–1121) studied under Roscellinus and Anselm of Laon, and was also a proponent of realism.
[
20
]
William was a friend of mystic
Bernard of Clairvaux
(1090–1153).
[
20
]
The philosophers of the
cathedral school at Chartres
were at the forefront of an intellectual climate of the
High Middle Ages
now known as the
twelfth-century Renaissance
, pioneering the
Scholastic
philosophy that came to dominate European medieval philosophy.
[
21
]
Known as
Chartrains
, they promoted scholarship and
Platonism
, such as found in the
Timaeus
.
[
22
]
[
23
]
Ivo of Chartres
(c. 1040–1115) was a student of Anselm at Bec.
[
24
]
The best known philosophers at Chartres included
Bernard
(d. c. 1125) and
Thierry
(d. c. 1150) of Chartres, and
Gilbert of Poitiers
(c. 1086 –1154).
[
22
]
Gilbert of Poitiers studied under William of Champeaux, Anselm of Laon and Bernard of Chartres.
[
25
]
Gilbert's views on the Trinity were controversial, contending the divine
essence
of God exists separately, and so he was condemned for teaching a "quaternity."
[
26
]
William of Conches
(c. 1090–c. 1154) studied under Bernard.
Herman of Carinthia
(c. 1105–c. 1155) and
Clarembald of Arras
(c. 1110–c. 1187) were among Thierry's students.
[
27
]
William of Champeaux was also the teacher of
Walter of Mortagne
(c. 1100–1174),
[
28
]
leader of the "indifferentists", a type of platonist who attempts to avoid the more extreme forms of platonism, and according to whom the universal it itself indifferent, changing according to points of view. Raimbert's nominalism was attacked by
Odo of Tournai
(1060–1113).
[
29
]
Peter Abelard
(1079–1142) was a scholastic
philosopher
,
theologian
and
logician
who taught at the cathedral schools of Paris. The
Chambers Biographical Dictionary
describes him as "the keenest thinker and boldest theologian of the 12th Century".
[
30
]
He wrote
Sic et Non
(c. 1121) and fixed more decisively than anyone before him the scholastic manner of philosophizing. Abelard was also expelled by Anselm of Laon, and clashed with his master William of Champeaux, and opposed by
Alberic of Paris
.
[
31
]
Abelard is also notable for his love affair and collaboration with
Héloïse
(1101–1164).
[
32
]
Abelard helped to establish the authority of
Aristotle
's
logic
.
[
33
]
Abelard distinguished between
de dicto
modal sentences and
de re
modal sentences.
[
34
]
Abelard also defended
conceptualism
on the problem of universals.
[
35
]
Abelard further showed a great interest in
ethics
, writing
Ethics
(1139).
[
36
]
Abelard amended
Augustine
's doctrine of
original sin
. The Vatican and
Pope Innocent III
accepted the view that unbaptized babies did not, as at first believed, go straight to
Hell
but to a special area of
limbo
,
limbus infantium
.
[
37
]
[
38
]
They would therefore feel no pain, but no supernatural happiness either, because they would not be able to see the deity who created them.
[
39
]
Abelard's lectures attracted students from across Europe, helping prepare the founding of the
University of Paris
a few decades after his death.
[
40
]
The patronage of Italian philosopher
Peter Lombard
(c. 1096–1160) by
Odo, bishop of Lucca
, who recommended him to Bernard of Clairvaux, allowed him to leave Italy and further his studies at Reims and Paris.
[
41
]
Lombard became
Bishop of Paris
and is author of the
Sentences
(c. 1150).
[
41
]
The
Petit Pont
school introduced the
new logic
, and included
Adam of Balsham
(c. 1100–c. 1157), who studied with Lombard, and
William of Soissons
, who coined the
principle of explosion
.
[
42
]
The
Summa aurea
of
William of Auxerre
(1150–1231) shows a debt to Lombard.
[
43
]
Bishop of Paris
William of Auvergne
(c. 1185–1249) extensively engaged with Aristotle.
[
44
]
Franciscan
John of La Rochelle
(c. 1200–1245) taught at Paris.
[
45
]
Italian philosopher
and founder of the Aristotelian
Thomist
school
Thomas Aquinas
(c. 1225–1274) taught at Paris.
John of Paris
(c. 1255–1306) defended Aquinas.
[
46
]
The
Condemnations of 1210–1277
at the recently founded
Sorbonne
,
Étienne Tempier
deemed Aristotle's
Physics
to be heresy, opening the door to modern science by questioning
ancient science
.
[
47
]
Averroists
Siger of Brabant
(c. 1240–c. 1284) and
Boethius of Dacia
have been singled out as the most prominent targets of the 1277 censure.
[
48
]
John of Jandun
(c. 1285–1328) was a later Averroist.
[
49
]
The enigmatic
Gerard of Brussels
probably published his pioneering study of
kinematics
Liber de motu
(
On Motion
) some time in the 13th century.
[
50
]
Lambert of Auxerre
was a contemporary logician.
[
51
]
A number of
Jewish philosophers
were in
Southern France
in the Middle Ages, such as
Samuel ibn Tibbon
(c. 1150–c. 1230), who wrote
Biur meha-Millot ha-Zarot
(1213), an explanation of the philosophical terms of
Guide for the Perplexed
(c. 1190) by
Maimonides
, which seeks to reconcile Aristotelianism with Rabbinical Jewish theology.
[
52
]
[
53
]
Gersonides
(1288–1344) was a rigid Aristotelian.
[
54
]
Catalan
Ramon Llull
(c. 1232–c. 1316) visited Paris in the 1280s and
Llullism
became popular. Llulism is a philosophical system known as 'the Art' which propounds a belief in the unity of Christianity influenced by neoplatonism.
[
55
]
While Llull was not himself an
alchemist
, a number of works on alchemy were attributed to him, as well as to
Arnaldus de Villanova
(c. 1240–1311).
[
56
]
[
57
]
Influenced by
Joachim of Fiore
, Arnaldus claimed that in 1378 the world would end and the
Antichrist
would come (
De adventu Antichristi
, 1288).
[
58
]
He was imprisoned and the Sorbonne ordered his works to be burned. Both Llull and Villanova had some influence on alchemist
John of Rupescissa
(c. 1310–c. 1368), known for
aqua vitae
.
[
59
]
[
60
]
The nominalist beliefs of British philosopher
William of Ockham
were banned in Paris in 1339.
[
61
]
[
62
]
Despite this his views proved influential.
Jean Buridan
(
c.
1301–c. 1360) was a nominalist who is the namesake for
Buridan's ass
. Buridan criticized Aristotle's
Physics
, which could not explain why e. g. an arrow in flight continues to move. Buridan in response developed the
theory of impetus
, a precursor to
inertia
.
[
63
]
Buridan was also considered one of the foremost logicians of the later Middle Ages. For 200 years after Buridan, little was said about
syllogistic logic
.
[
34
]
Nicole Oresme
(1325–1382) studied with Buridan. Together they studied
acceleration
or "uniformly difform motion".
[
64
]
Oresme was a counselor of King
Charles V
.
[
65
]
Oresme practiced astronomy, and his commentary on Aristotle's
De Caelo
(
On the Heavens
) anticipated Copernicus with arguments for the view that the Earth rotates.
[
66
]
[
67
]
Oresme also criticized Aristotelian notions of
space and time
, considering time independent of motion, perhaps influenced by, or at least agreeing with, the views of prior scholars
Peter John Olivi
(1248–1298) and
Gerardus Odonis
(1285–1349).
[
68
]
[
69
]
Oresme also contributed to
economics
and followed Aristotle in arguing against
usury
,
[
70
]
even though Oresme said
inflation
was worse.
[
71
]
His opposition to usury was shared by Thomists like
Giles of Lessines
(c. 1230–c. 1304), as well as
Giles of Rome
(c. 1243–1316) student Italian
Gerard of Siena
(c. 1295–1336),
[
72
]
and Peter John Olivi and Gerardus Odonis; and his master Buridan.
[
73
]
[
74
]
[
75
]
[
76
]
Buridan and Oresme supported a
metallist
theory of money.
[
71
]
The nominalist and skeptical views of
Nicholas of Autrecourt
(c. 1299–1369) and
John of Mirecourt
, known as
Monachus Albus
('the White Monk'), were condemned as heresy in 1347. Both wrote commentaries on the
Sentences
; and both rejected the notion of
causality
and the Aristotelian ideas of
substance theory
.
[
77
]
Mirecourt influenced
Peter Ceffons
.
[
78
]
Pierre d'Ailly
(1351–1420) was a nominalist who taught the
Sentences
.
[
79
]
His pupils were
Jean Gerson
(1363–1429) and
Nicholas of Clémanges
(c. 1360–1440). All three philosophers were embroiled in the
Western Schism
of 1378, and taught Ockham's
conciliar theory
.
[
80
]
Jean Gerson developed
natural rights
theory, and also defended the divine mission of
Joan of Arc
.
[
81
]
University of Toulouse professor and physician
Raymond Sebond
(1385–1436) opposed the Ockhamists and was influenced by Llull. He attempted to reconcile reason and faith. Raymond declares that the
Book of Nature
and the
Bible
are both divine revelations.
[
82
]
Sebond wrote the posthumously published
Theologia naturalis
(1484).
16th century
Italian
Renaissance humanist
Gregory of Tifernas
was the first teacher of Greek in France at the
University of Paris
in 1458.
[
83
]
Guillaume Fichet
(1433–c. 1480) and
Robert Gaguin
(1434–1501) are usually seen as the first
French humanists
.
[
84
]
Guillaume Budé
(1467–1540) was another French humanist.
[
85
]
French Renaissance humanist
Rabelais
(c. 1490–1553) contributed to French philosophy in
Gargantua
and
Pantagruel
a belief in
hedonistic
man uncorrupted by institutions, and ridiculed
Pyrrhonism
in the third book (1546).
[
86
]
Logician and education reformer
Petrus Ramus
(1515–1572) wrote
Quaecumque ab Aristotele dicta essent, commentitia esse
(
Everything that Aristotle has said is false
, 1536). The Ramists distrusted human thought and put faith in intuitive logical relations.
[
87
]
The
Dialogues
(1557) of
Ramist
Guy De Bruès
(b. c. 1530) entertained skepticism.
[
88
]
[
89
]
The first writings on Ramism after the death of Ramus included biographies, such as by
Banosius
and
Nancelius
.
[
90
]
[
91
]
Ramism had a lasting influence in Europe and even
New England
.
[
92
]
[
93
]
France also saw a
Protestant
movement following the
Reformation
, such as the
Huguenots
, led by
John Calvin
(1509–1564), the founder of
Calvinism
, which believes in
predestination
and
salvation
through God alone (
monergism
).
[
94
]
Calvin wrote
Institutes of the Christian Religion
(1536).
[
95
]
The Huguenots had precursors in such philosophers as Llullist
Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples
(c. 1455–c. 1536).
[
96
]
Jean Bodin
(c. 1530–1596) was critical of papal authority, preferring the
sovereignty
of an
absolute monarch
during the
Wars of Religion
.
[
97
]
Ramus was a Protestant convert and a victim of the
St. Bartholomew's Day massacre
.
[
98
]
Budé's family fled from France.
[
85
]
Henri Estienne
(1531–1598) was responsible for the first printed Latin translation of the works of Pyrrhonian
skeptic
Sextus Empiricus
in 1562.
[
99
]
Michel de Montaigne
(1533–1592) was a skeptic, summed up in his personal motto of
Que sais-je?
("what do I know?")
[
100
]
His highly influential writing style consists of
essays
('attempt', he coined the term) first published in 1580, filled with autobiographical and casual anecdotes.
[
101
]
Montaigne's best known skeptical essay is the circuitous
Apology for Raymond Sebond
, which recapitulates much from Sextus Empiricus, but while defending Christianity and the
cosmological argument
.
[
102
]
Montaigne maintains beasts and savages are better off than people. He propounded cultural
primitivism
in
Of Cannibals
.
[
103
]
Montaigne was friends with political philosopher
Étienne de La Boétie
(1530–1563), author of the posthumously published
Discourse on Voluntary Servitude
(1577).
[
104
]
Montaigne also influenced moralist
François de La Rochefoucauld
(1613–1680).
[
105
]
Montaigne's follower was the Parisian and
neostoic
Pierre Charron
(1541–1603), who was also influenced by
Guillaume du Vair
(1556–1621).
[
106
]
Charron is notable for
On Wisdom
(1601), which argued that ethics could be separated from religion, and that one attacks reason to boost faith and wisdom.
[
107
]
[
108
]
Charron also wrote
The Three Truths
(1594), in which Charron sought to prove that
God
exists,
Christianity
is true, and the true church is
Roman Catholicism
.
Francis Garasse
(1585–1631) criticized Charron, believing he thought only nature was needed for wisdom and guidance.
[
107
]
University of Toulouse
professor
Francisco Sanches
(c. 1550–1623) published the skeptical
Quod nihil scitur
(
That Nothing Is Known
, 1581).
[
109
]
While Sanches does not develop the idea, he states there needs to be a method based on indubitable inner experience.
[
109
]
17th century
France in the early modern period
became the cultural center of Europe, especially under the reign of "Sun King"
Louis XIV
, and saw a number of prominent philosophers.
[
110
]
Louis XIV's tutor was
libertine
François de La Mothe Le Vayer
(1588–1672).
Libertines
were such skeptics that they believed the more knowledge, the more grief.
[
111
]
[
112
]
[
c
]
Philosophy at this time often sought to reconcile
dogmatism
and skepticism.
[
113
]
Modern philosophy
began in France with
René Descartes
(1596–1650), who raised problems central to 17th century thought. An expat who lived in the
Dutch Republic
, he studied at the
Jesuit
school
La Flèche
and was a pioneer of mathematics and the
Scientific Revolution
.
[
114
]
Descartes founded a
mechanistic philosophy
known as
Cartesianism
which incorporated his own
Cartesian physics
. His philosophy was also
rationalist
and
dualist
, supported in works like
Meditations on First Philosophy
(1641) and
Discourse on Method
(1637). The three great rationalists of early modern philosophy are Descartes,
Baruch Spinoza
, and
German philosopher
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
(1646–1716).
[
115
]
It is often said Descartes changed the primary object of philosophical thought from
ontology
to
epistemology
.
[
116
]
Descartes was concerned with the recent spread of skepticism, and desired to find
indubitable ground
on which all the sciences could be placed and progressively built. Thus he
doubted
anything he could and accepted only
certain
(or
apodeictic
) knowledge as truth.
[
117
]
After invoking the possibility of
dreaming
to doubt the information given to him from his
senses
and the
external world
, and further of an
omnipotent deceiver
to reject the information given to him from mathematics and logic, Descartes discovered at least one thing could be known for certain. Even if he doubted everything, if he himself was doubting, then he had to exist. Thus
Cogito Ergo Sum
—I think, therefore I am. This became his
first principle
.
[
118
]
[
119
]
Descartes then claimed that because he discovered the
Cogito
through perceiving it "
clearly and distinctly
", anything he can similarly perceive as clearly and distinctly must be true. Then he argues that he can conceive of an infinite being, but finite beings cannot produce infinite ideas and hence an infinite being must have put the idea into his mind. He uses this argument, commonly known as an
ontological argument
, to invoke the existence of a benevolent God as the indubitable foundation that makes all sciences possible.
[
120
]
Cartesianism attracted several followers such as
Jansenist
solitaires
Antoine Arnauld
(1612–1694) and
Pierre Nicole
(1625–1695). Together they produced the
Port-Royal
Logic
(1662), the "most influential logic book after Aristotle and before the end of the nineteenth century".
[
121
]
In 1649,
Nicolas Cornet
(1572–1663) sought the condemnation of five propositions from
Cornelius Jansen
's
Augustinus
. Arnauld defended the Jansenists.
[
122
]
Cornet's student
Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet
(1627–1704) supported the king's revocation of the
Edict of Nantes
(
Edict of Fontainebleau
, 1685), abolishing the rights of the Protestant minority.
[
123
]
Bossuet also banned the work of
Oratorian
Richard Simon
(1638–1712), who was influenced by
Pre-Adamite
theorist
Isaac La Peyrère
(1596–1676).
[
124
]
[
125
]
Other Cartesians were physiologist
Louis de La Forge
,
[
126
]
Géraud de Cordemoy
,
[
127
]
[
128
]
Claude Clerselier
,
[
129
]
University of Paris professor
Edmond Pourchot
,
[
130
]
recollect
Antoine Le Grand
,
[
131
]
mystic
Pierre Poiret
,
[
132
]
physicist
Jacques Rohault
,
[
133
]
Bernard de Fontenelle
,
[
134
]
Robert Desgabets
,
[
135
]
Pierre-Sylvain Régis
,
[
136
]
and
François Poullain de la Barre
.
[
137
]
François Poullain de la Barre (1647–1723) influenced
Gabrielle Suchon
(1632–1703), the first to produce a significant body of work solely on the topic of women.
[
138
]
Claude Buffier
(1661–1773) supported women's education.
[
139
]
While Descartes drew many followers, others were left unsatisfied. Some accused him of
circularity
, proclaiming his ontological argument uses his definition of truth as a premise, while his proof of his definition of truth uses his ontological argument as a premise.
[
140
]
Another famous
problem
arises from Descartes’ substance dualism; the interaction problem first pointed out by
Princess Elizabeth of Bohemia
.
[
141
]
For Descartes, a
substance
can be conceived of as existing independently of anything else. He defined the
mind
as an unextended substance and the body as an
extended
substance.
[
142
]
This raised the fundamental question of how it is possible that mind and body interact with one another.
[
143
]
Descartes also held as a result of his dualism that
animals were mere machines
.
[
144
]
The
Minim
and polymath
Marin Mersenne
(1588–1648) wrote
The Truth of Science
(1625), a dialogue between an
alchemist
, a skeptic and a Christian philosopher, the latter opposing both the over-confidence of the first and the excessive doubts of the second. The rest of the book is an 800 page compilation of mathematics to prove there is knowledge immune from doubt.
[
145
]
[
d
]
Mersenne is notable as the father of
acoustics
and the namesake for
Mersenne primes
. He was "the center of the world of science and mathematics during the first half of the 1600s,"
[
147
]
and, because of his ability to make connections between people and ideas, "the post-box of Europe".
[
148
]
As well as in France, Mersenne corresponded with scholars in the
Dutch Republic
, England, and Italy, including
Constantijn Huygens
,
Thomas Hobbes
, and
Galileo Galilei
.
[
148
]
Blaise Pascal
(1623–1662) was a child prodigy mathematician and scientist who grew increasingly religious.
[
149
]
Pascal was a
vacuuist
who repeated the
barometric
mercury
experiments of Italian
Evangelista Torricelli
,
[
150
]
while Descartes was a plenist who held "

Pascal is known for defending Jansenism and Arnauld in

152

When Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet was asked which work he wished he had written aside from his own, he answered the

.

153

Pascal was also a
fideist
, and distinguished between using the head and using the heart. His aphoristic collection
Pensées
(Thoughts, 1670) is a name given posthumously to fragments that Pascal had been preparing of an
apology
for Christianity, which was never completed.
Pensées
contains
Pascal's Wager
.

Pascal's Wager is an early application of the mathematics of
probability
, and says people engage in a life-defining
gamble
regarding the belief in the existence of God.

155
]
Pascal was a Cartesian dualist, illustrated with a quote from the
Pensées
: "Man is only a
reed
, the weakest in nature, but he is a thinking reed." However, his disagreements can be illustrated by his calling Descartes' philosophy "useless and uncertain".

Cartesian
Nicolas Malebranche
(1638–1715) believed not even substances of the same kind could interact with each other, because no necessary
causation
could be perceived. He proposes then that it is God, an uncreated substance, who brings it about that each time one perceives a 'cause', one also perceives an 'effect'. Hence the doctrine is named
occasionalism
.
[
157
]
This doctrine saw predecessors in Louis de La Forge (1632–1666), Géraud de Cordemoy (1626–1684), and the Flemish
Arnold Geulincx
.
[
158
]
Malebranche was well-known and celebrated in his own time, but has since become somewhat of an obscure figure. However, his philosophy had a direct influence upon
Spinoza
, and Scottish skeptic
David Hume
's questioning of causality, which awoke German idealist
Immanuel Kant
from his "dogmatic slumber."

Pierre Gassendi
(1592–1655), the most influential anti-Cartesian in France, argued against
innate ideas
. Gassendi sought to revive the
ancient atomism
of
Epicureanism
, and was also a nominalist and a skeptic. Gassendi was an acquaintance of nominalist Thomas Hobbes.
[
160
]
Gassendi was a member of the
libertins érudits
(
free thinker
) discussion group, which included playwright and duelist
Cyrano de Bergerac
, scholar
Henri Louis Habert de Montmor
, librarian
Gabriel Naudé
, and physician
Guy Patin
.

states Gassendi was one of the first to formulate the modern "scientific outlook".

Gassendi tracked the
transit of Mercury
in 1631, using the predictions of German
Johannes Kepler
's
Rudolphine Tables
(1627), projecting an image from a

onto a screen.

Pierre Bayle
(1647–1706) was a Huguenot at the
Academy of Sedan
, who fled to
Rotterdam
in the Dutch Republic, and wrote a
biographical dictionary
, the
Historical and Critical Dictionary
(1697). His views were dubbed "super skepticism" by Richard Popkin. Bayle would characterize his own views differently, stating "I know too much to be a Pyrrhonist, and I know too little to be a Dogmatist".

Bayle's comments on the
problem of evil
inspired Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, who wrote in Latin and French, to publish his
Théodicée
(1710).

174

Leibniz was an
optimist
who believed God created the
best of all possible worlds
. Bayle was also an influence on David Hume.

18th century
The 18th century saw the French
Enlightenment
and nearby
Swiss Enlightenment
.
[
176
]
French Enlightenment philosophers, known as
philosophes
, were deeply political, and many became critics of church and state, and promoters of rationality and progress.
[
177
]
They had a deep influence on the politics and ideologies of both the
American Revolution
and the
French Revolution
.
Marquis de Lafayette
(1757–1834) supported both revolutions.
[
178
]
Philosophy was discussed in
salons
, often led by
salonnières
such as
Marie Thérèse Geoffrin
,
Madame Lambert
, or
Jeanne Julie Éléonore de Lespinasse
.
[
179
]
Charles de Secondat, baron de Montesquieu
(1689–1755) was a social commentator and political philosopher. His theories deeply influenced the
American Founders
. His belief that the state powers be separated into
legislative
,
executive
, and
judicial
branches formed the basis for
separation of powers under the United States Constitution
.
[
180
]
In
The Spirit of the Laws
(1748), Montesquieu outlined the view that man and societies are influenced by
climate
. He believed that hotter climates create hot-tempered people and colder climates aloof people, whereas the mild climate of France is an ideal balance.

h

François-Marie Arouet, better known as
Voltaire
(1694–1778), was a prominent Enlightenment figure who advocated the right to a free trial and freedom of religion. Voltaire was a
deist
, and was twice sentenced to prison, and once to temporary exile to England.
[
182
]
A heavy influence on the
Enlightenment
was the work of British natural philosopher
Sir Isaac Newton
and the philosophy of
Newtonianism
, who published his
Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica
(1686), which included
his laws of motion
, introducing
classical mechanics
in
physics
.
[
183
]
Voltaire and
Émilie du Châtelet
(1706–1749) wrote
Elements of the Philosophy of Newton
(1738), helping to popularize Newtonianism in France alongside
Pierre Louis Maupertuis
(1698–1759).
[
184
]
Châtelet was the first woman published by the
French Academy of Sciences
. Voltaire's
Letters on the English
(1734) introduced French readers to the philosophy of the
British empiricists
like Newton and
John Locke
, as well as to playwright
William Shakespeare
.
[
185
]
Voltaire is best remembered today for his aphorisms and his satire of Leibniz known as
Candide
(1759), written soon after the
1755 Lisbon Earthquake
,
[
186
]
which tells the tale of a young believer in Leibnizian optimism who becomes disillusioned after a series of hardships.
Voltaire's anonymously published
Philosophical Dictionary
(1764) was censored in many countries, including Switzerland (
Geneva
) and France, where all available copies of the book were collected and burned in the town square.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau
(1712–1778) distinguished himself from the progressive
scientism
of the Enlightenment with his proclamation in
Discourse on the Arts and Sciences
(1750) that art and science are corruptors of human morality.
[
189
]
Furthermore, he caused controversy with his theory that man is good by nature but corrupted by society, in contradiction to the Christian doctrine of original sin.
[
190
]
Rousseau's
The Social Contract
(1762) advances
social contract
theory and states that only the
general will
of the people has the right to legislate. It famously begins “Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.” Upon publication, the distribution of
The Social Contract
in France was prohibited, and Rousseau fled the country to avoid imprisonment.
[
191
]
However it influenced the French Revolution. Rousseau was so highly praised by the French revolutionists that in 1794 his remains were moved to the
Panthéon
in Paris. Rousseau's
Emile
(1762) had previously been forbidden and publicly burned, but became the basis of a new national system of education.
[
192
]
His picture was the only one to grace the home of Immanuel Kant.

193

Some of his theories continue to be controversial, such as his idea of the general will, which has been accused of both fascism and communism.
